summary: Describes the AppleTalk Update-based Routing Protocol (AURP), which improves AppleTalk routing over wide area links and stays compatible with AppleTalk Phase 2. It is informational.

eli5.summary: AppleTalk is a network for Apple computers. This memo explains how those networks can talk over long distances by only sending news when something changes.

questions: appletalk routing over wide area networks
subtitle: Connect Apple networks over long distances by tunneling through IP and sharing routing updates efficiently.

tldr.problem: AppleTalk networks worked well for local area networks but did not scale efficiently to wide area networks. The standard Routing Table Maintenance Protocol (RTMP) created heavy traffic and could not support very large networks over long distances.
tldr.mechanism: AURP allows AppleTalk networks to be tunneled through foreign networks (like IP) to reach distant AppleTalk networks. It uses an update-based routing protocol instead of RTMP's periodic broadcasts, sending routing information only when the topology changes, reducing traffic dramatically.
tldr.outcome: AppleTalk networks can now be interconnected globally over TCP/IP internets, leased lines, and point-to-point links while remaining compatible with existing AppleTalk Phase 2 routers and protocols.

today: RFC 1504 is an Informational RFC documenting the AppleTalk Update-Based Routing Protocol. While AppleTalk networks are no longer widely deployed in modern networks, AURP remains a reference for how to design update-based routing protocols for wide area networks and how to tunnel non-IP protocols through IP internets.

sections.title: AppleTalk Goes Wide Area
sections.content: AppleTalk Update-Based Routing Protocol (AURP), documented in RFC 1504, enables AppleTalk networks—originally designed for local area networks (LANs)—to scale to wide area networks (WANs). AURP is fully compatible with AppleTalk Phase 2 and consists of three major components: tunneling (encapsulating AppleTalk data to pass through foreign networks like TCP/IP), routing information propagation (exchanging routing state between distant routers), and network information presentation (how local routers present remote network information). The protocol solves a fundamental problem: the standard AppleTalk routing protocol, RTMP (Routing Table Maintenance Protocol), generates high traffic overhead on slow wide area links because it periodically broadcasts entire routing tables. AURP replaces this with update-based routing, sending routing information only when network topology changes.
sections.eli5: AppleTalk was made for networks in one building. AURP adds features so AppleTalk networks can talk across the world. Instead of constantly sending all routing information, AURP only sends news when something changes, which uses much less bandwidth.

sections.title: Tunneling Through Foreign Networks
sections.content: Tunneling is the first major component of AURP. An exterior router sits on the boundary between an AppleTalk internet and a foreign network (such as TCP/IP, X.25, or a point-to-point link). When forwarding AppleTalk data across the tunnel, the exterior router encapsulates it with the headers required by the foreign network and adds an AURP-specific domain header that identifies the source and destination AppleTalk domains. The router then sends the encapsulated packet through the foreign network to another exterior router, which decapsulates it and forwards it to its destination AppleTalk network. AppleTalk tunnels can be dual-endpoint (point-to-point, connecting exactly two routers) or multipoint (connecting two or more routers on a shared tunnel). On multipoint tunnels, exterior routers use split-horizon routing, sending each other only information about their own local networks and never re-exporting information learned from other routers on the tunnel. This prevents routing loops.
sections.eli5: Imagine AppleTalk data packets are letters. An exterior router puts each letter in a protective envelope (with the foreign network headers) and a label (the domain header) saying where the letter comes from and where it is going. It mails this envelope through the Internet or a phone line to another exterior router, which opens the envelope and delivers the letter to the right AppleTalk network.

sections.title: Update-Based Routing Information Exchange
sections.content: The second major component of AURP is the routing information propagation mechanism. Instead of periodic broadcasts like RTMP, AURP uses an update-based approach: exterior routers exchange routing information only when the network topology changes. The protocol defines two key exchange phases: an initial information exchange (when two routers first meet) and incremental updates (whenever routing information changes). During the initial exchange, each exterior router sends complete information about its local network to peers. Thereafter, when a network becomes reachable or unreachable, or when a route metric changes, the router sends a targeted update to its peers. AURP routers maintain split-horizoned routing state, meaning each router stores a separate copy of the routing information for each other exterior router's local internet. The protocol also supports mechanisms like router-down notification (letting peers know when a router is shutting down) and zone information exchange (mapping network numbers to zone names), which is essential for AppleTalk's naming system.
sections.eli5: Instead of all routers constantly broadcasting their entire route table every few seconds (which wastes bandwidth), AURP routers only send messages when something changes. If a network goes down or a new route appears, the router announces that change. This is like having mail carriers only show up with route updates when roads actually change, not every 10 seconds.

sections.title: Optional Features for Large Networks
sections.content: Beyond the core tunneling and routing propagation, AURP supports optional features that help manage large WANs. Network hiding lets an exterior router hide specific networks from remote internets for security and traffic reduction. Network-number remapping resolves conflicts when two distant AppleTalk networks use the same network number. Hop-count reduction allows routers to adjust metrics, enabling much larger networks than standard RTMP (which limits distance to 15 hops). Internet clustering treats a group of networks as a single entity on the WAN, minimizing routing information. Hop-count weighting and backup paths allow administrators to optimize traffic across multiple routes. Device hiding provides additional security by hiding specific routers from remote networks. These features are optional, allowing implementations to start simple and add capabilities as needed.
sections.eli5: AURP also has tricks for handling big networks. You can hide some networks for privacy, pretend multiple networks are one to reduce chatter, allow very long paths (more hops), and set up backup routes if the main path fails.

sections.title: Packet Formats and Domain Identifiers
sections.content: AppleTalk data packets sent across AURP tunnels are preceded by foreign-protocol headers (such as IP/UDP for IP tunneling) and a domain header. The domain header contains a version field, a packet type field (distinguishing data packets from routing packets), and two variable-length domain identifiers—one for the source and one for the destination. Domain identifiers uniquely identify AppleTalk internets on a tunnel. The simplest form is the null domain identifier (used when distinction is not needed, such as on point-to-point links). For IP tunnels, the domain identifier is derived from the IP address of the exterior router, eliminating manual configuration. The domain header is omitted when both domain identifiers would be null, saving overhead. RFC 1504 specifies the exact bit layouts for these headers, including handling of fragmentation when AppleTalk packets exceed the foreign network's maximum transmission unit (MTU).
sections.eli5: Each message traveling through a tunnel gets a special wrapper with sender and destination labels (domain identifiers), a version number, and a type mark saying whether it is data or routing information. The wrapper structure depends on what kind of tunnel is being used, but they all work the same way.

sections.title: State Machines and Network Management
sections.content: The appendix of RFC 1504 provides state diagrams for AURP operations, including connection setup, routing table exchange, and error handling. AURP defines error codes that routers use to signal problems (such as invalid packets or security errors) to peers. The protocol also specifies how routers handle edge cases: partial tunnel connectivity (when not all routers on a multipoint tunnel can directly reach each other), AURP table overflow (when the number of routes exceeds capacity), and schemes for efficient updates after initial information exchange. Implementation guidance covers topics like free-trade zone creation (for backward compatibility with pure RTMP networks) and modified RTMP algorithms for backup path support. The specification is designed to be implementable on various platforms and to coexist with existing AppleTalk infrastructure.
sections.eli5: AURP describes exactly how routers talk to each other: handshake sequences, error messages, and what to do if something goes wrong. It also explains how to handle special cases like when routers cannot reach each other directly, or when the routing table gets too big.
